chapters.title: SHA3-256: compact vs. Oxide Quartz
chapters.narration: This demo compares SHA3-256: the compact core in this project, and Oxide’s Quartz implementation. Here’s how the input architecture changes speed and resource use.

chapters.title: AXI Stream into the Quartz core
chapters.narration: A sixty-four-bit AXI stream feeds each core. In the Quartz integration, a local adapter feeds one byte per clock into two full block buffers. One fills while the other feeds the hash state. Twenty-four permutation rounds produce the result, which is copied into a separate digest register.

chapters.title: Compact: absorb directly into the state
chapters.narration: The compact core uses that same stream interface. It captures up to eight bytes at a time, then absorbs them directly into the hash state with an aligned exclusive-or. The two full block buffers disappear. The digest comes directly from the held state, so that separate register disappears too. Capture and absorption still take separate cycles. The twenty-four-round permutation is unchanged.

chapters.title: Refinement 1: padding selection
chapters.narration: Two smaller changes simplify the compact core further. First, padding. Compare this project's earlier wide core with the compact version. Previously, a variable index selected from all twenty-five state lanes. The compact version decodes the destination locally, across only the seventeen rate lanes that padding can touch. The eight capacity lanes remain in the hash state; padding leaves them alone.

chapters.title: Refinement 2: validate before absorption
chapters.narration: Second, input validation. The earlier design checked the byte mask and end-of-message flag on the state-update control path. The compact core records that check while capturing the input. On the next cycle, a bad word is rejected before absorption. These changes reduce surrounding logic. They preserve the hash algorithm and the simulated cycle count.

presentation_style: One generic AXI Stream input; upstream sources introduced only in the later replay experiment.
